common_name: Crassinervium Anthurium (Thick-Veined Anthurium, Florida Strap Anthurium)

planting.note: Propagate by division of offsets at the base of the rosette, or by removing and rooting basal suckers in spring when new growth begins; seedlings are slow and rarely used in cultivation.

directions: Anthurium crassinervium forms a clustered, bird's-nest-like rosette of leathery, glossy, deep green, oblanceolate leaves, with strongly raised primary lateral veins radiating out from the midrib in a distinctive pattern that gives the species its Latin name ("thick-veined"). It is native to the Caribbean and northern South America and has become a staple understory and foundation planting in South Florida and Caribbean landscapes because of its comparative sun and drought tolerance relative to velvet-leaf collector anthuriums. Grow in filtered sun to part shade with rich, well-drained soil outdoors, or in bright indirect light with a chunky aroid mix as a container specimen. It tolerates brief dry spells and lower humidity better than most bird's-nest anthuriums, making it a forgiving choice for beginner growers.

planting.note: Propagate by division of basal offsets or by rooting a stem section with at least one node in warm, humid, chunky aroid mix; new growth establishes fastest in spring and summer warmth.

directions: Anthurium digitatum produces palmately divided leaves with several finger-like lobes radiating from a central point, giving it a bold, sculptural silhouette distinct from the solid heart- or strap-shaped leaves of most collector anthuriums. Its divided-leaf form places it alongside Anthurium clavigerum and Anthurium pedatoradiatum, though digitatum is generally more compact and self-heading rather than climbing. Grow in bright indirect light with a very well-drained, chunky aroid mix, and maintain moderate to high humidity for the fullest lobe development; leaves that emerge in low humidity tend to be smaller and less deeply divided. This species is grown almost entirely for its unusual leaf architecture rather than its modest aroid inflorescence.

planting.note: Propagate by stem cuttings with aerial roots, or by division of clustered stems; roots readily in damp sphagnum or chunky aroid mix under warm, humid conditions.

directions: Anthurium gracile is a slender, clambering epiphyte with narrow, glossy lanceolate leaves and a widespread range through Central and South America and the Caribbean. It is grown as much for its ornamental fruit as its foliage: small spadices develop into clusters of berries that ripen a bright orange to red, held above the leaves for weeks at a time. Its compact, wiry habit and tolerance of lower light make it a good candidate for terrariums, vivariums, and hanging baskets rather than as a large specimen plant. Grow in bright indirect light with high humidity and a fast-draining, chunky mix or mounted on bark to encourage aerial roots.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow as a greenhouse or high-humidity collector specimen; propagate only by division of an established plant, since it is exceptionally slow from tissue culture or seed and rarely offered.

directions: Anthurium reginae is a rare Ecuadorian velvet-leaf species belonging to the same general group of large pendulous or semi-pendulous velvet anthuriums as A. warocqueanum and A. veitchii, with big, deeply veined, dark green leaves and a soft, matte, velvety texture. It is exceptionally slow-growing and seldom offered in the trade, making it one of the most sought-after "grail" species among serious aroid collectors. Grow mounted or in a hanging position with very high humidity, warm consistent temperatures, strong air circulation, and bright filtered light, replicating cloud-forest conditions as closely as possible; it does not tolerate the fluctuating humidity and dry air of an average home without supplemental humidification.
sources: specialty aroid nursery and collector references

common_name: River Anthurium (Amnicola Anthurium, Dwarf Strap-Leaf Anthurium)

planting.note: Propagate by dividing offsets from the compact clustering base; establishes quickly in a small pot with a light, well-drained aroid or terrarium mix.

directions: Anthurium amnicola is a compact, clustering species with narrow, strap-shaped, glossy leaves; its Latin epithet references a streamside or riverbank habitat in Central America. Its small mature size and persistent papery cataphylls make it well suited to terrariums, vivariums, and windowsill culture, and it has been used as a breeding parent for compact, strap-leaf hybrid anthuriums valued for their manageable scale. Grow in bright indirect light with consistently moist, fast-draining mix and elevated humidity; unlike many larger strap-leaf species it stays small enough to thrive long-term in a modest container.

common_name: Leathery Anthurium (Coriaceum Anthurium, Brazilian Leather-Leaf Anthurium)

planting.note: Propagate by division of basal offsets from a mature rosette; slow to establish but tolerant of brief handling and root disturbance thanks to its thick, leathery foliage.

directions: Anthurium coriaceum forms a large, architectural rosette of thick, glossy, elongated paddle-shaped leaves with a stiff, leathery (coriaceous) texture, native to Brazil's Atlantic Forest region. The thick cuticle that gives the species its name also makes it noticeably more tolerant of brighter light and lower humidity than most velvet-textured collector anthuriums, making it a comparatively forgiving choice for growers moving beyond andraeanum hybrids. Grow in part shade to bright indirect light with a well-drained, chunky mix; established plants can handle short dry-downs between waterings without the rapid decline typical of thinner-leaved velvet species.

planting.note: Propagate by stem cuttings with aerial roots taken below a node, rooted in warm, humid conditions against a moss pole or similar climbing support.

directions: Anthurium ochranthum is a vigorous, hemiepiphytic climbing species with large, glossy, leathery leaves and a distinctive yellow-orange spathe and spadix, a flower color unusual enough among anthuriums that the species has been used by breeders seeking warm-toned color in ornamental hybrids. Provide a moss pole or other rough support for the climbing stems, since aerial roots need something to grip for the plant to reach its full mature leaf size. Grow in part shade to bright indirect light with consistent moisture and high humidity; younger plants kept without a climbing support stay noticeably smaller and produce fewer flowers than specimens allowed to climb.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
